_comment: What this repository is allowed to say about the world outside it. Read by
scripts/check_disclosure.py, which fails when the published tree mentions anything not
This is an ALLOW-list on purpose. A deny-list of things that must not be published would
have to name them -- and a public file naming the private hosts and projects it is guarding
against is itself the disclosure it claims to prevent. An allow-list contains only values
already intended for publication, so publishing the policy costs nothing.
Adding an entry is a deliberate act. If this check fails on a new address or host, the
question to answer is 'should this be public?' -- not 'how do I make the check pass?'.
forbidden_patterns holds only vendor-generic shapes: API surfaces and filesystem shapes
that are wrong to publish regardless of who owns them. Nothing private is named here.

forbidden_patterns.why: An organisation-scoped API call reads account state that is wider than this repository and, for some fields, is visible only to members. Scope verification commands to the repository.
GET /orgs/{org} returns the billing plan only to members. Publishing it discloses account information no reader of this repository needs.
An organisation-wide security posture field. State this repository's own security_and_analysis instead.
Names the tier or plan this account holds. Say that a paid tier is required and link the vendor's documentation; which tier is held adds nothing a reader can act on.
An absolute path from a maintainer's own machine. Publish repository-relative paths.
An absolute home directory reveals an operator account name. Publish repository-relative paths.
An absolute macOS home directory reveals an operator account name.
